name: New Atheism
scope: The early-2000s movement of popular, openly confrontational critics of religion, centred on the books of Richard Dawkins, Daniel Dennett, Sam Harris and Christopher Hitchens (the 'Four Horsemen'; Johnstone also counts Victor Stenger): religion in general, not any one doctrine, is held to be false and harmful, and public life, education and policy are to be guided by rational argument and scientific evidence rather than supernaturalism (s1, s2, s3, s4). The Stanford Encyclopedia notes that scholars have no agreed definition and that the label names a movement united mainly by timing and popularity, not a distinct philosophical position (s2); it came from journalism (s3, s5). Scope is the core works of these authors from 2004 to 2007 and what the defining sources report of their tenets. It excludes older atheism (Hume, Russell, Marx), state atheism and Soviet 'scientific atheism', and the critics' own positions (Feser, Lennox, Johnstone use the label to argue against it; they define it, not hold it).

summary: New Atheism is the label for the mid-2000s wave of best-selling books by Dawkins, Dennett, Harris and Hitchens that treat religion in general as false and socially harmful. Its authors hold that public life and education should rest on reason and scientific evidence, that morality needs no religion, and that creationism, theocracy and blasphemy or apostasy laws are to be opposed. Scholars note it has no agreed definition beyond this shared criticism of religion.
